doc.title: Butch Miles interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, October 9, 2020 [interview 2 of 2]

chapter: Playing, records and the Hyman album
title: How his playing has changed, from Basie and Brubeck to Mulligan
summary: Working in varied styles pushed Butch to play more subtly, especially in Gerry Mulligan's quartet and big band. Mulligan's groups always had piano, such as Harold Danko and Bill Mays.

story.theme_name: Leading a band: choosing, paying and managing players
story.community_name: Leading a band: running, choosing and keeping players

blocks.x: Okay. Do you feel your playing has changed over the years either out of necessity or out of choice?

Yes, yes and yes. It has changed over the years. And some of it has been out of necessity because I had worked for the first four and a half years where I — for wont of a better phrase — made my bones, I was working with the Basie band. And that’s where I got my reputation. Then the next thing I turned around, as you remember, and I joined up with Dave Brubeck’s quartet. (How could he do that?) Well it was easy for me because I was raised on both Basie and Brubeck. Then later I started playing with other groups, more trad oriented, more, definitely solid in the 1940s swing oriented, and a few other bands

that were of a different type of, oh I don’t know what the word would be, a connotation for a musical genre or a style, and I found that I just couldn’t stay in one particular crevice, a musical crevice as it were. I couldn’t apply what I’ve always been playing to (A) when the band was playing let’s say (B) I had to think of something else to play. So I would have to switch and it got me to thinking and got me to changing my style because I had to. And then later on I found that there was so much enjoyment in playing so many different ways and so many different things that it was by my choice. I started experimenting and playing different styles and different rhythms and different beats. I still had my old cliches and they’re still there, you can’t get rid of them. But I was more adventurous. I didn’t have to stay so stuck in any one particular rut anymore. I could go all kinds of different ways. And so I did that by choice. So my playing right now is quite different, not totally different, but it’s quite different from what you might hear in 1975, 1977.
Is it possible to be specific about one part of your playing that is different?

I don’t state the beat so hard anymore. I don’t pound at you. I’ve learned to get up off that bass drum and use that as a musical voice more often but I still use it as the bottom line in connection with a good walking bass player, not so much to beat somebody up with but just to give a little bit more support to. And use my feet, both feet, as other voices so that I try to think of now, I try to think in more musical terms, percussive terms. I think I got slaughtered on that thing when I was working with Gerry Mulligan and a quartet back in the 80s, and I did a number of gigs with him and the big band, and his big band, some of it, is on YouTube, some very fine TV shows came out of oh I don’t know where it’s — Italy I think, and we did a number of things with the quartet and a number of things with the big band and I found I had to change my playing style to work with Gerry, and I enjoyed it very much. So I began to re-educate myself, I didn’t have to drive so hard all the time. There was something nice to be said for subtlety.
Was that a group without a chordal instrument?

No, no. The ones that I played in with Gerry always had a piano. Harold Danko was on the band for a long time, Bill Mays, the wonderful Bill Mays was there. It was always basically Gerry, piano, bass and drums.
